stem: A data scientist wants to see whether the continuous feature `trip_distance` in a large trips table is heavily right-skewed and whether it has several clusters of values. In a Databricks notebook, which visualization answers this most directly?

choices.text: A histogram of `trip_distance` with an adjustable number of bins
A counter display showing the average `trip_distance`
A word cloud built from the `trip_distance` column values
A pie chart of `trip_distance` bucketed into ten equal slices

stem: An analyst needs to compare how the continuous feature `fare_amount` is spread within each value of the categorical feature `payment_type`, including medians, quartiles and extreme values per category. Which visualization fits best?

choices.text: A pie chart with one slice for each `fare_amount` value, sized by row count
A line chart of `fare_amount` ordered by row number
A scatter chart with `payment_type` on both axes
A box chart of `fare_amount` by `payment_type`

stem: Before training a classifier, a practitioner wants to check how balanced the three values of the categorical label `churn_segment` are in a table with 50 million rows. Which approach gives the clearest picture without changing the query that produces the table?

choices.text: A scatter chart with a point for each of the 50 million rows
A box chart of `churn_segment` with the median shown for each row
A bar chart of row counts per `churn_segment`, using chart aggregation
A histogram of `churn_segment` with many narrow bins to show fine detail

stem: A practitioner displays a 12-million-row DataFrame as a table and builds a bar chart of the average `price` per `region` by adding the chart to the result. The averages look slightly different from a `groupBy("region").avg("price")` run on the same data. The visualization is configured with no aggregation and uses the displayed rows as they are. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Spark `avg` ignores rows where `region` has more than one letter
The chart is built from the table's first 64,000 displayed rows, not from the whole dataset
Bar charts always round the averages to whole numbers before drawing the bars
The notebook cache was cleared, so the chart reads stale data from a previous cluster

stem: Which TWO visualizations show the distribution of a single continuous feature in a Databricks notebook? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Word cloud
Pie chart
Histogram
Counter display
Box chart

stem: A practitioner wants to measure how strongly two continuous features, `age` and `annual_income`, move together in a Spark DataFrame, assuming a roughly linear relationship. Which statistic fits best?

choices.text: The mode of each column compared side by side
A chi-squared test of independence between the two raw columns
The count of distinct values in each column
The Pearson correlation coefficient between the two columns

stem: A practitioner has two categorical columns, `plan_type` and `churned` (both converted to numeric category indices), and wants to test whether they are statistically independent. Which Spark ML tool is designed for this?

choices.text: `OneHotEncoder` with `dropLast=False` on `churned`
`ChiSquareTest.test(df, "features", "label")` on the indexed categorical values
`Imputer` with `strategy="mode"` on both columns
`Correlation.corr(df, "features", "spearman")` on the two indexed columns, read as an independence test

stem: A practitioner wants to decide whether the mean of the continuous feature `session_minutes` differs between two groups defined by the categorical feature `app_version` (versions "A" and "B"). Which statistical comparison matches this combination of feature types?

choices.text: A two-sample t-test on `session_minutes` between the two groups
A Pearson correlation between `app_version` and its own indexed value
A bar chart of the distinct values of `session_minutes`
A chi-squared test of independence on `session_minutes`

stem: A practitioner computes the Pearson correlation between `x` and `y` and gets about 0.02, yet a scatter chart shows `y` rising sharply as `x` moves away from zero in either direction (a U shape). What is the correct interpretation?

choices.text: The scatter chart must contain an error, because a U shape cannot produce a coefficient near zero
The features are unrelated, because a coefficient near zero proves independence
Pearson correlation is always wrong for continuous data and should be replaced by the mean
The relationship is strong but nonlinear, and Pearson only measures linear association

stem: Two numeric features in a training set have a Pearson correlation of 0.97, and a linear regression model shows unstable coefficients. Which TWO actions are reasonable? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Drop one of the two highly correlated features
Impute the missing values of both features with the mode
Switch to Spearman correlation to remove the dependency between them
Apply one-hot encoding to both numeric features
Replace both with one combined feature, for example a principal component or a ratio

stem: The column `household_income` is strongly right-skewed with a few very large values and has about 4% missing values. The practitioner wants a single fill value that is not pulled by the extreme incomes. Which statistic should be used?

choices.text: The mean of the non-missing values
The median of the non-missing values
The mode of the non-missing values
The maximum of the non-missing values

stem: The categorical column `payment_method` (strings such as "card", "cash", "voucher") has missing values. Which fill strategy is appropriate?

choices.text: The mean of the category counts, rounded to the nearest label
The median of the string lengths of the category labels
The most frequent category (the mode)
The mean of the category labels after sorting them alphabetically

stem: A column `sensor_temp` is symmetric (roughly normal) with no outliers and a small share of missing values. A reviewer asks why mean imputation is acceptable here. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Mean imputation adds new row-specific information about each missing record
Mean imputation increases the variance of the column because it adds more rows
The mean is always more robust to outliers than the median, so it is safer
Mean and median nearly coincide, so the fill leaves the center essentially unchanged

stem: Which TWO statements about mean imputation of a numeric feature are true? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The column's mean after imputation equals the mean of the values that were present
The values filled in are different for each row, based on its neighbors
It is the right choice for categorical columns stored as strings
It strengthens the correlation of the imputed feature with every other feature
It shrinks the column's variance because filled rows all sit at the center

stem: A practitioner fills missing `age` values using the median of the entire dataset and only then splits it into training and test sets. The test metric is later found to be slightly optimistic. What is the most accurate reason?

choices.text: The split changed the data type of `age` from double to string, so the evaluation was biased
The fill value used test rows, so test information leaked into preprocessing
Spark cannot split a DataFrame after a column has been imputed, so the split was approximate
Median imputation always inflates metrics regardless of when the split is done

stem: A practitioner runs this code on a DataFrame whose `age` column contains `null` values and some `NaN` values. ``` imp = Imputer(strategy="median", inputCols=["age"], outputCols=["age_imp"]) out = imp.fit(df).transform(df) ``` What does `age_imp` contain for the rows where `age` was null or NaN?

choices.text: Zero, because no fill value was set explicitly
Null for the null rows and the median for the NaN rows
The median of the non-missing `age` values for both kinds of rows
The mean of the non-missing `age` values for both kinds of rows

stem: Missing values in a numeric column `distance` were stored by the source system as `-999` instead of null. Which Imputer configuration replaces them with the column median?

choices.text: `Imputer(strategy="mean", missingValue=0.0, inputCols=["distance"], outputCols=["d"])`
`Imputer(strategy="median", relativeError=0.999, inputCols=["distance"], outputCols=["d"])`
`Imputer(strategy="mode")` with default settings
`Imputer(strategy="median", missingValue=-999.0, inputCols=["distance"], outputCols=["d"])`

stem: A practitioner calls `Imputer(strategy="mode", inputCols=["city"], outputCols=["city_imp"])` on a string column `city` that has missing values, and the job fails or gives wrong output. What is the correct way to fill the missing cities with the most frequent city?

choices.text: Set `missingValue` to the empty string, which makes Imputer accept text
Change the strategy to `mean`, which supports string columns
Take the top city of `groupBy("city").count()` and `df.fillna({"city": top})`
Cast `city` to `float` first, then rerun Imputer so strings are read as numbers

stem: A practitioner fits an `Imputer(strategy="median")` on the training DataFrame and saves it inside a pipeline model. At scoring time a new batch has missing `age` values. Which statement describes the correct behavior?

choices.text: The pipeline recomputes the median from the scoring batch each time it runs
The fitted model applies the training median to the new batch
The fitted model fills the gaps with the mean of the scoring batch itself
Scoring fails because Imputer only works while a model is being trained

stem: Which statement about `pyspark.ml.feature.Imputer` is correct?

choices.text: It offers mean (default), median and mode on numeric columns
It supports only the strategy mean on any column type
It is a plain transformer that needs no fit step and keeps every column unchanged
Its default strategy is median and it works on string columns

stem: A categorical feature `colour` (red, green, blue) has no natural order. It is encoded as the integers 0, 1, 2 and fed to a logistic regression. Why is one-hot encoding preferable?

choices.text: Integer codes imply green sits between red and blue, an order and spacing that do not exist
Logistic regression cannot read numeric columns at all
Integer codes use the least memory of any encoding, so the model always trains faster
One-hot encoding guarantees that the feature will be normally distributed

stem: A training pipeline has a string column `country` and numeric columns `age` and `income`. In what order should the Spark ML stages run to produce one feature vector for a logistic regression?

choices.text: OneHotEncoder, then StringIndexer, then VectorAssembler
VectorAssembler, then OneHotEncoder, then StringIndexer
StringIndexer, then VectorAssembler, then OneHotEncoder
StringIndexer, then OneHotEncoder, then VectorAssembler

stem: `OneHotEncoder(inputCols=["idx"], outputCols=["vec"])` is applied with default settings to a column `idx` that has 5 categories (indices 0 to 4). What does the row with `idx = 4` become?

choices.text: A vector of length 1 containing the value 4.0
A vector of length 4 where every entry is 0.0
A vector of length 5 where every entry is 1.0
A vector of length 5 with a one in position 4

stem: A model trained with `StringIndexer` and `OneHotEncoder` fails at scoring time with an error when a new batch contains a country that was not in the training data. What change prevents the failure and keeps the batch in the output?

choices.text: Convert the country to lower case before scoring, so each new country maps to a known one
Drop the `OneHotEncoder` stage so that unseen values are not encoded
Set `handleInvalid="keep"` on the `StringIndexer` and refit, so unseen values get an extra index
Set `dropLast=False` on the encoder only, which hides unseen strings

stem: Which TWO statements about Spark ML `OneHotEncoder` are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It can transform several columns at once with `inputCols` and `outputCols`
It replaces missing values with the mean of the column
It reads raw string columns directly without a prior indexing step
It keeps every category as a column by default, with `dropLast=False`
It maps a category index to a binary vector with at most a single one

stem: A team already uses Ray on its Databricks Runtime ML cluster for parallel compute and wants a hyperparameter tuning library that runs on that same distributed backend. Which library fits?

choices.text: Optuna, a framework for dynamic search spaces that scales with Joblib and tracks trials in MLflow
MLlib `CrossValidator`, which evaluates a fixed parameter grid with Spark jobs for Spark ML pipelines
Hyperopt with `SparkTrials`, which sends each trial to a Spark worker and is no longer maintained
Ray Tune, the tuning library that comes with Ray and uses Ray as its backend for distributed computing

stem: A team tunes a Spark MLlib `RandomForestClassifier` on a very large DataFrame with Optuna on a recent Databricks Runtime ML. Each model fit already spreads its work over every executor. How should the trials be scheduled?

choices.text: Replace the MLlib model with a scikit-learn model collected on the driver, so trials can overlap
Run the trials one after another, so each distributed fit can use the whole cluster
Run 64 trials at once on the executors, each starting its own distributed fit inside a worker task
Cache a separate copy of the DataFrame for every trial, so that the trials never compete for executors

stem: A team moves tuning to a recent Databricks Runtime ML and wants to define the search space inside the objective function with calls such as `trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-4, 1e-1, log=True)`, then run many trials tracked in MLflow. Which library does that pattern belong to?

choices.text: Hyperopt, where the search space is built inside the objective with `trial.suggest_*` calls and `SparkTrials` is required
Spark MLlib's `ParamGridBuilder`, where each parameter value is declared as a `suggest` call on the estimator
Optuna, where the objective function receives a trial object and uses suggest methods to declare the search space
scikit-learn's `GridSearchCV`, where the objective function is replaced by an estimator and an evaluation metric

stem: A team uses Optuna on a recent Databricks Runtime ML to run parallel studies on Spark executors, with every trial logged to one MLflow experiment. Which TWO elements does the Databricks documentation use for this setup? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `CrossValidator`, a Spark MLlib class that replaces the Optuna sampler with a fixed parameter grid scored by k-fold validation
`SparkTrials`, passed to `optuna.create_study` to distribute trials to workers
`fmin()` with `algo=tpe.suggest`, wrapped around the Optuna objective function
`MlflowStorage`, so that all workers share one Optuna storage backed by the MLflow tracking server
`MlflowSparkStudy`, whose `optimize` call launches parallel Optuna studies on PySpark executors

stem: Runtime upgrade planning shows that a team's distributed tuning code relies on Hyperopt `SparkTrials`. According to the Databricks documentation, what should the team move to?

choices.text: AutoML only, because manual hyperparameter tuning libraries are no longer supported on Databricks
MLlib `CrossValidator` only, because it is the single supported hyperparameter tuning tool after Hyperopt
Optuna, which can run parallel studies on Spark, or Ray Tune, as the documented replacements
Plain Python loops over `fmin()`, since newer Databricks Runtime ML versions ship a rewritten and actively maintained Hyperopt

stem: A model has six hyperparameters, and one training run takes 20 minutes. A grid search with 8 values per hyperparameter was planned, but the team can afford only about 60 training runs in total. Which search strategy is the best fit?

choices.text: Exhaustive grid search, accepting a run time of several years on a single machine
Random search or Bayesian optimization with the budget set to 60 trials
Grid search on the first two hyperparameters only, leaving the other four at their defaults
Grid search with 2 values per hyperparameter, since a grid is the only strategy that guarantees fair coverage

stem: A tuning job uses a Bayesian optimizer (TPE) with a fixed budget of 100 trials. How does it differ from random search with the same budget?

choices.text: It chooses each new setting using the results of earlier trials, so later trials concentrate on promising regions
It needs no objective function, because the model's loss is estimated from the training data statistics alone
It evaluates every possible combination first and then discards the worst ones before the budget is reached
It samples every setting independently from the space, so earlier results never influence later suggestions

stem: A data scientist tunes an L2 regularization strength that could reasonably be anywhere from 0.00001 to 100, and a tree depth between 3 and 12. How should the regularization strength be sampled in a random or Bayesian search?

choices.text: As a categorical choice of the three values 0.00001, 1 and 100, to keep the search small
As an integer between 1 and 100, rounded after sampling, to avoid very small floating-point values
Uniformly between 0.00001 and 100, so that every number in the range is equally likely
On a log scale, so each order of magnitude gets about the same share of the trials

stem: A team tunes a random forest with three hyperparameters (number of trees: 3 values, max depth: 4 values, minimum samples per leaf: 2 values). Training takes seconds, and the team wants a result that is reproducible and tests every combination. Which strategy fits?

choices.text: Random search with one trial per hyperparameter, so each parameter is tested once
Grid search, because 3 x 4 x 2 = 24 combinations is small and every combination is evaluated exactly once
Random search with 5 trials, because fewer trials always generalize better
Bayesian optimization, because it is the only method that systematically tests every possible combination in the space

stem: A data scientist wants to find good hyperparameters for a scikit-learn gradient-boosting model. The training data fits in memory on a single node, one fit takes 4 minutes, and 200 trials are planned. A cluster with 32 worker cores is available. What approach shortens the tuning time without changing the model?

choices.text: Increase the number of folds in cross-validation to 32, so the 32 workers are all used
Run the 200 trials one after another on the driver, because a single-node model cannot use a cluster
Run many trials at once on the workers with a trial-distributing tool such as Optuna on Spark or Ray Tune
Convert the model to Spark MLlib's `GBTClassifier` first, which is a drop-in replacement with identical results

stem: A team uses a Bayesian optimizer with a fixed budget of 128 trials. Raising concurrency from 4 to 64 parallel trials makes the job much faster, but the best loss found is slightly worse. What explains this?

choices.text: Higher concurrency makes each new suggestion rely on fewer completed results, so the optimizer is less adaptive
The optimizer switches to grid search whenever more than 16 trials run at once
Parallel trials are evaluated with a smaller share of the training data, which makes their losses less accurate
Higher concurrency cuts the number of trials that the optimizer is allowed to run, so fewer settings are evaluated overall

stem: A retailer must train a separate scikit-learn forecasting model for each of 3,000 stores, and each store's data is small. A Spark DataFrame holds all stores with a `store_id` column. How can the work run in parallel on the cluster?

choices.text: Use `df.groupBy("store_id").applyInPandas(train_fn, schema)` so each store is fitted by `train_fn`
Collect the DataFrame with `toPandas()` and loop over the stores on the driver
Fit one MLlib model on all rows and give `store_id` as a numeric feature
Broadcast the whole DataFrame to the driver memory, then call `fit` once with `store_id` as the label column

stem: A team runs Optuna on Spark workers, but each trial function reads a 40 GB table with `spark.table(...)` inside the objective, and trials fail or run extremely slowly. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Move the objective function to the driver and call `spark.table(...)` there once for each worker node
Keep calling `spark.table(...)` inside the objective, as before, but raise the parallelism to the number of cells in the table
Put the data where workers can read it, such as a cloud storage path or a small broadcast sample, and load it in the objective
Raise the cluster's driver memory to 40 GB so that all workers can read the Spark session

stem: Which TWO statements are true about running parallel tuning trials for single-node models on a Databricks cluster? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A trial for a single-node model should be wrapped inside an MLlib `Pipeline` so Spark can split its fit over executors
Parallel trials always return the same best result as sequential trials of the same budget, whatever the algorithm
Increasing parallelism beyond the number of available task slots keeps speeding up the job without limit
The number of trials that can run at the same time is limited by the task slots available on the workers
Each trial is one independent model fit, so trials can be spread over different workers and run concurrently

stem: A team has 600 million labeled rows and wants to tune a Spark MLlib model with a large parameter grid on a limited compute budget. Which validation method is the better choice and why?

choices.text: `CrossValidator` with `numFolds=2`, because two folds are equivalent to a train-validation split
`TrainValidationSplit`, because it fits each setting once and one large validation set is a reliable estimate
`CrossValidator` with `numFolds=10`, because more folds always give a better model whatever the data size
No validation at all, because the final model is evaluated on the training data

stem: A dataset has only 900 labeled rows. Two hyperparameter settings differ by one percentage point of accuracy on a single 80/20 validation split. Why is k-fold cross-validation the better choice here?

choices.text: It removes the need for a final test set and for any hyperparameters
It trains only once, so it is faster than a single split on small data
It guarantees the setting with the best average will give the best accuracy on all future data
It averages the metric over k validation sets, using every row once, which gives a steadier comparison

stem: A forecasting team has two years of daily sales and uses random k-fold cross-validation to compare models. Offline scores are excellent, but production error is much higher. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: Time series models cannot be validated at all, so the offline scores carry no information
Random k-fold always overfits the hyperparameters, so it cannot be used for any kind of data
Random folds put future rows in training data for earlier validation rows, which inflates the score
The number of folds was too small, so the model never saw all of the rows

stem: Which TWO statements correctly compare k-fold cross-validation with a single train-validation split? (Select TWO)

choices.text: k-fold cannot be combined with hyperparameter grids, which is why a single split is used for tuning
k-fold cross-validation fits each hyperparameter setting k times, so it costs about k times more training than one split
A single split always selects a better model than k-fold because it keeps more rows for training
A single split gives a lower-variance estimate than k-fold because its validation rows never change
k-fold evaluates every row as validation data exactly once, so its averaged metric depends less on one lucky split

stem: A fraud model has 0.5 percent positive labels. With random 5-fold validation on 2,000 rows, some folds contain almost no fraud cases and the fold metrics swing widely. What improves the validation?

choices.text: Use stratified folds that keep the same class ratio in every fold
Sort the rows by label and assign contiguous blocks to folds
Remove all negative rows from the validation folds, so only fraud rows are scored
Reduce the number of folds to 1, so there is no variation between folds

stem: A data scientist must pick the regularization of a Spark ML `LogisticRegression` through 5-fold cross-validation. Which items must the `CrossValidator` receive?

choices.text: An estimator, a list of parameter maps built with `ParamGridBuilder`, and an evaluator
A trained model, a test DataFrame, and a loss function written in SQL
A Delta table name and a primary key column, which are used to create the folds
Only a DataFrame, because `CrossValidator` discovers the model type and metric on its own

stem: A pipeline chains `StandardScaler` and `LogisticRegression`. A data scientist first fits the scaler on the full training DataFrame, transforms it, then runs `CrossValidator` on the scaled data. Validation scores are slightly optimistic. What is the better design?

choices.text: Fit the scaler on the validation fold only, so that the scaling reflects the data being scored
Pass a `Pipeline` of scaler and classifier as the estimator, so the scaler is refit on each fold's training part
Fit the scaler on the full dataset including the test set, to give every fold identical statistics and scaling
Remove the scaler from the pipeline, since scaling never matters for logistic regression

stem: What does this scikit-learn code return? scores = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(), X, y, cv=5, scoring="f1")

choices.text: One F1 score, calculated on all five folds pooled together into a single combined validation set
A fitted random forest trained on the best of five hyperparameter settings
A confusion matrix for each of the five folds
An array of five F1 scores, one per fold, usually summarized with `scores.mean()`

stem: A team tunes a Spark ML pipeline with a 3 x 2 parameter grid and 3-fold `CrossValidator`. The cluster has spare capacity, but the job runs the models one at a time. What can speed it up?

choices.text: Collect the training DataFrame to the driver so that each fold trains in a pandas process
Set the `numFolds` value to 1, so that Spark runs fewer fits than the grid requires
Set the `parallelism` parameter of `CrossValidator` to a value of 2 or more, within the cluster's resources
Convert the grid to a Python list and loop in the driver, which is always faster than CrossValidator

stem: After `cv_model = cross_validator.fit(train_df)` completes, which TWO statements about the result and the process are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The final model is refit on the test DataFrame, which was therefore used to select the parameters
Each model is fitted on its validation fold and then scored on the remaining training folds
`cv_model.bestModel` was refit using the best parameter map on the entire training DataFrame
`cv_model` contains only the first fold's model, because the other folds' models are discarded and never evaluated
Each parameter map is scored with the average of the metrics from the models fitted on its k folds

stem: Two tuning jobs have the same 80-trial budget for a gradient-boosted model with 10 hyperparameters, but only two of them strongly affect accuracy. One job evaluates 80 cells of a grid with 3 values per hyperparameter, the other draws 80 independent random settings. Why is plain random search usually better at finding good values of the two important hyperparameters?

choices.text: Each random trial draws a new value of every hyperparameter, so 80 trials test 80 distinct values of each, not 3
Random search trains each model for more epochs, which increases accuracy in every trial
Random search ignores the unimportant hyperparameters, so it never needs to set a value for any of them in a trial
Random search always picks values that the grid cannot contain, so it finds exact optima

stem: A retail company is setting up MLOps on Databricks with Unity Catalog. Data scientists experiment freely, an ML engineering team runs automated tests, and only a locked-down process may touch production. Which design follows the Databricks recommendation for isolating these stages?

choices.text: Use a single development workspace for everything and mark the stage of each model version by moving it between the legacy registry stages "Staging" and "Production"
Create a separate execution environment per stage (development, staging, production) with its own compute and jobs, and a matching catalog for its data and models
Separate only the production environment, and let development and staging share one catalog so that test results are visible to the data scientists immediately
Keep one shared catalog for all ML assets and tell the stages apart with "dev_", "test_" and "prod_" prefixes on table and model names

stem: In most situations, which approach does Databricks recommend for moving an ML solution from development to staging and production?

choices.text: Promote the evaluation metrics only and re-train the model by hand in production when the numbers look good
Promote the data from the development catalog and let each environment generate its own pipeline code on the fly
Promote the trained model artifact from environment to environment, so that the exact binary tested in staging is the one served in production
Promote the training code, so the production model is trained by production code that passed review and integration tests

stem: A team follows Databricks recommendations for MLOps on Unity Catalog. Which TWO practices match that guidance? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Store raw data and feature tables as files in a shared cloud folder so that each team can choose its own format
Keep training notebooks in each data scientist's personal workspace folder and copy them to the production workspace when a model looks good
Give every data scientist write access to the prod catalog so that fixes can be applied to production features without a pipeline
Track training with MLflow and manage model versioning, governance and deployment status with models in Unity Catalog
Store pipelines and project code in Git, using Databricks Git folders to sync with the workspace, so moving ML logic between stages means moving code between branches

stem: A validation job loads a newly trained model from Unity Catalog and runs format checks, required-metadata checks and performance checks on selected data slices. The model passes every check. What does the recommended Databricks workflow do next?

choices.text: The model is assigned the "Challenger" alias so a deployment step can promote it to "Champion" or compare it with the current Champion
The model stage is moved to "Production" in the legacy registry, which immediately starts serving traffic
The model is deleted from the catalog and re-registered under the name of the production model, replacing its earlier versions entirely
The AutoML data exploration notebook is regenerated so that reviewers can approve the model

stem: A security policy prevents data scientists from reading anything in the production catalog, but they still need realistic data to develop and evaluate project code. What does Databricks suggest as an alternative?

choices.text: Grant the data scientists the same permissions on production tables as the production jobs, but only on weekends
Write a snapshot of the production data to the development catalog, where data scientists have read-write access
Copy the production training code into the production catalog and let data scientists develop there under shared accounts
Ask the data scientists to generate random numbers that match the column types and develop against those only

stem: What is the main purpose of the staging stage in the recommended Databricks MLOps workflow?

choices.text: To hold a permanent backup copy of the production model and its feature tables so they can be restored if the production catalog is ever lost or damaged
To let data scientists explore data interactively in notebooks and decide which features may be useful
To run unit and integration tests in CI over all ML pipeline code, then cut a release branch that starts production
To serve the model to real users for the first time and gather business feedback before any tests run

stem: A team trains models with scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch and keeps losing time installing matching library versions on new clusters. Which benefit of Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning addresses this most directly?

choices.text: It replaces Spark with a single-node engine, so no library versions have to match
It creates compute with pre-built, tested ML and deep learning libraries, kept current for top-tier ones
It converts every scikit-learn and XGBoost model into a Spark ML model automatically at training time
It trains any model on a GPU without code changes, as long as the library is installed on the driver

stem: A data scientist selects the "Machine learning" option when creating classic compute and then reads tables from Unity Catalog in a notebook. Which access mode does Databricks set automatically, and why does it matter?

choices.text: Dedicated, assigned to the creating user; Unity Catalog access on the ML runtime needs it
Standard, shared by all workspace users; this is the only mode that allows Unity Catalog on the ML runtime
No isolation shared, which lets the cluster read Unity Catalog tables without checking privileges
Serverless, which removes the need for an access mode and bills only for queries

stem: A team enables Photon on compute running Databricks Runtime ML and sees no speed-up when training a scikit-learn RandomForest and an XGBoost model on a pandas DataFrame, though their Spark SQL feature engineering became faster. What explains this?

choices.text: Photon is disabled on Dedicated access mode, so every query ran on the standard engine
Photon only works with tables stored outside Unity Catalog, so the training data must be moved out of it
Photon speeds up Spark SQL and DataFrame work, but not Python packages such as XGBoost
Photon requires GPU instance types for model training, so CPU training never benefits from it

stem: A workflow needs an extra Python library on Databricks Runtime ML. Which TWO statements about adding libraries are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An init script can only install libraries for the driver node and never for workers
Adding any extra library is blocked on Runtime ML, since the runtime image cannot be extended
A notebook-scoped library installed with %pip is shared by all notebooks attached to the same compute
A notebook-scoped Python library is available only to that notebook's session, which keeps other users' environments unchanged
A compute-scoped library makes the library available to all notebooks running on that compute

stem: A team will fine-tune a large deep learning model on GPUs and has been running it on Databricks Runtime ML GPU compute. What does the current Databricks guidance say for custom deep learning workloads such as fine-tuning?

choices.text: Move the work to Photon-enabled CPU compute because Photon accelerates PyTorch training
Use AI Runtime, a serverless GPU compute offering optimized for deep learning, instead of Runtime ML
Keep using Runtime ML on classic GPU compute because serverless GPU does not support deep learning workloads
Use AutoML, which is the recommended tool for fine-tuning deep learning models on GPUs

stem: An analyst gives AutoML a labeled customer table and asks for a classification experiment with the label column as target. How does AutoML find a good model?

choices.text: It trains and tunes models across several algorithms (trees, forests, logistic regression, XGBoost, LightGBM) and presents the best trial
It fits a single logistic regression and reports its coefficients as the final model
It copies the architecture of the last model registered in Unity Catalog and retrains that one with the new data
It asks the user to choose one algorithm and then only tunes the learning rate for that choice

stem: A planner has two years of weekly sales with strong yearly seasonality and needs a baseline for the next 12 weeks. Which AutoML problem type is appropriate, and which algorithms does it try on classic compute?

choices.text: Clustering; it groups weeks by similarity and uses the cluster mean as the forecast
Regression; it only trains linear regression with stochastic gradient descent
Forecasting; it trains Prophet and Auto-ARIMA models and compares them
Classification; it predicts the next week as a class using decision trees

stem: Before launching a classification experiment, an analyst notices the table contains a customer_id column that carries no signal and should not be used as a feature. Which action fits what AutoML supports?

choices.text: Nothing can be done; AutoML always uses every column of the input table
Delete the target column from the table so AutoML will use the id column as the label instead
Rename the id column to "label" so AutoML ignores it during feature selection
Exclude customer_id in the configuration; the target and time-split columns must stay

stem: A churn dataset has demographics only. The team already maintains a Unity Catalog feature table with recent usage metrics per customer. How can AutoML use it?

choices.text: Replace the input dataset with the feature table; AutoML does not accept a separate labeled dataset
Use existing feature tables to augment the input dataset through the feature store integration
AutoML cannot read other tables, so the usage metrics must be exported to CSV and appended by hand
Register the feature table as a model so AutoML can pick it up as a baseline

stem: A risk team wants to know which input features most influence the model AutoML selects, using Shapley values. What do they need to know about AutoML-generated notebooks?

choices.text: Shapley values are computed only for forecasting models and cannot be produced for classification or regression models at all
Shapley values are always computed during training and stored in the data exploration notebook
The notebooks include SHAP code, off by default because it is memory-intensive; set shap_enabled = True and re-run
Shapley values need a separate paid add-on and cannot be generated in generated notebooks

stem: A regulated lender uses AutoML for a first model but must show auditors the exact preprocessing and training code and tweak the best model by hand. Which AutoML benefit applies?

choices.text: AutoML hides the model internals behind a managed service, which protects the intellectual property of the lender
AutoML exports the model only as a compiled binary that cannot be edited
AutoML automatically submits the model to regulators and files the documentation
AutoML generates a source code notebook for the best trial, so the team can review, reproduce and modify the code

stem: Which TWO benefits do data scientists get from running AutoML at the start of a project? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It records each trial as an MLflow run with parameters, metrics and the model, so trials can be compared and the best one registered
It guarantees a better model than any hand-built one on every dataset, so manual modeling work is no longer needed
It deploys the best model to a production serving endpoint automatically and routes all traffic to it
It removes the need to evaluate a model on held-out data because it always predicts perfectly
It quickly produces baseline models and a data exploration notebook that summarizes the dataset, which speeds up exploratory analysis

stem: After an AutoML classification experiment finishes, a data scientist can see the notebook for the best trial in the workspace, but cannot find workspace notebooks for the other trials. Where are they?

choices.text: They are saved as artifacts of each trial's MLflow run, to be downloaded and imported by hand
They were never generated, since AutoML writes source code for the best trial only
They sit on the cluster driver's local disk and were deleted when the experiment compute shut down
They are inside the model files in Unity Catalog and can be read by loading the model

stem: A team pip-upgrades scikit-learn on their Databricks Runtime ML cluster (a runtime version that includes AutoML) to a newer version for another project, and all AutoML runs on that cluster then fail. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The upgrade filled the driver's memory, which AutoML needs for the SHAP step in every run
AutoML only runs on serverless compute, so any classic cluster fails once a library is changed on it
AutoML requires an empty cluster with Python 2, and the upgrade changed the interpreter
AutoML needs the preinstalled library versions; changing them breaks compatibility

stem: An analyst compares AutoML with training one model by hand in a notebook. In which case does AutoML give the clearest advantage?

choices.text: Reproducing a published research model that uses a custom loss function and architecture
Choosing a business metric and deciding how costly a false positive is for the use case at hand and its customers
Exploring many algorithm and hyperparameter combinations on a new dataset, with each trial logged
Running a one-time SQL aggregation on a table to build a dashboard

stem: In Unity Catalog, what makes a Delta table usable as a feature table with Databricks Feature Store?

choices.text: It is stored in a catalog whose name ends in "_features"
It has a primary key constraint, so a row can be looked up by key
It uses Liquid Clustering on every column
It has been registered as a model version with the alias "features"

stem: Team A's feature table lives in the legacy Workspace Feature Store in one workspace. Team B, in another workspace of the same company, needs the same features. How do feature tables in Unity Catalog improve on this?

choices.text: It is accessible to all workspaces assigned to the table's metastore, with permissions managed in Unity Catalog
Unity Catalog feature tables are copied to each workspace's local storage whenever a new workspace is created
Unity Catalog feature tables remove the need for access control, because everyone in the account can edit them
Unity Catalog feature tables can only be read by the workspace that created them, but at least they are encrypted

stem: Which TWO benefits do feature tables in Unity Catalog have over workspace-level feature tables? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Features are automatically recomputed at every query without any pipeline or schedule
Feature tables are stored in a proprietary binary format that is faster than Delta
Access to feature tables is governed with Unity Catalog privileges, like other data assets, instead of a workspace-only control
Feature tables no longer need a primary key, because Unity Catalog generates one automatically when needed
Lineage between feature tables, functions and the models trained from them is tracked and can be viewed in Catalog Explorer

stem: A data engineer already maintains a Delta table customer_attrs in Unity Catalog, with one row per customer_id and no constraints. A data scientist wants to use it as a feature table for model training. What is required?

choices.text: Export the table to the legacy Workspace Feature Store so the key can be defined there
Add a primary key constraint on customer_id with ALTER TABLE; no separate feature store copy is needed
Recreate the table as a new Delta table in a catalog named "feature_store" and copy the data over
Convert the table to a materialized view so Databricks can index it for lookups

stem: A compliance officer asks which models were trained with a customer feature table before a column in it is changed. Which capability of Unity Catalog feature tables answers this?

choices.text: The model's alias, which stores the names of all training tables
The cluster event log, which records every table read by a notebook
The AutoML data exploration notebook, which lists every downstream model that read the table
Lineage tracked when models are trained with Feature Engineering in Unity Catalog, viewable in Catalog Explorer

stem: A team ran 60 hyperparameter trials that each logged a metric named `rmse` to the experiment with ID `1234`. A notebook cell must return only the single run with the lowest `rmse` as a pandas DataFrame. Which call does this?

choices.text: `mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], order_by=["metrics.rmse DESC"], max_results=1)`
`mlflow.get_run("1234")` followed by a sort of its `data.metrics` dictionary by value
`mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], order_by=["metrics.rmse ASC"], max_results=1)`
`mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=["1234"], filter_string="metrics.rmse = MIN")`

stem: Several training runs in one experiment log `val_accuracy`. The team wants the run with the highest `val_accuracy` programmatically with MLflow. Which TWO approaches return that run? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Read `mlflow.get_experiment(exp_id).best_run` after the trials finish, because the experiment object tracks its top run
Call `mlflow.last_active_run()` after the final trial, because it returns the run with the best metric in the current session
Call `mlflow.search_runs([exp_id])` without `order_by` and take the first row, because MLflow ranks returned runs by their best metric
Call `mlflow.search_runs([exp_id], order_by=["metrics.val_accuracy DESC"], max_results=1)` and read the single row of the returned DataFrame
Call `MlflowClient().search_runs([exp_id], order_by=["metrics.val_accuracy DESC"], max_results=1)` and take the first element of the returned list

stem: A notebook runs `best = mlflow.search_runs(["1234"], order_by=["metrics.rmse ASC"], max_results=1)`. The next cell must pass the best run's ID and its logged `max_depth` hyperparameter to the registration step. Which code reads them?

choices.text: `best.loc[0, "run_id"]` and `best.loc[0, "params.max_depth"]`
`best["run_id"]` and `best["max_depth"]`
`best.info.run_id` and `best.data.params.max_depth`
`best[0].info.run_id` and `best[0].data.params["max_depth"]`

stem: A data scientist runs `mlflow.search_runs(["1234"], filter_string="rmse < 1.0 AND team = 'fraud'")`. The call fails with a parse error although runs with `rmse` metrics and a `team` tag exist. What is the fix?

choices.text: Pass the conditions as a dictionary such as `{"rmse": "<1.0", "team": "fraud"}` instead of a string
Prefix each key by its kind: `metrics.rmse < 1.0 AND tags.team = 'fraud'`
Move the `rmse` condition into `order_by`, because metrics cannot appear in a filter string
Add a leading `WHERE` keyword, because the filter string is parsed as the condition of a SQL query

stem: A deep learning run logged `val_loss` once per epoch for 50 epochs. On the experiment page of the MLflow UI, the engineer wants to list only runs where `val_loss` fell to 0.2 or lower at some epoch, even if it rose again by the last epoch. Which search expression does this?

choices.text: `LOWEST(metrics.val_loss) <= 0.2`, which is the keyword for the minimum
`MIN(metrics.val_loss) <= 0.2`, which tests the lowest value in the metric history
`metrics.val_loss <= 0.2`, which tests the lowest logged value of each run
`params.val_loss <= 0.2`, because every epoch value is saved as a parameter

stem: A team uses `mlflow.sklearn.autolog()` for scikit-learn training. Autologging records parameters, training metrics and the model, but the team also needs a confusion matrix plot and a business metric `expected_revenue_lift` in each run. What should they do?

choices.text: Keep autologging and add `mlflow.log_metric("expected_revenue_lift", v)` plus `mlflow.log_figure(fig, "cm.png")` in the run
Write the plot and the value to a Delta table instead, because runs accept only values produced by the library itself
Disable autologging and recreate everything by hand, because autologging blocks custom logging calls inside the same run
Wrap the extra values in model hyperparameters, because autologging accepts custom values only through estimator parameters of the model

stem: A training loop logs `mlflow.log_param("learning_rate", 0.1)` once and `mlflow.log_metric("loss", loss, step=epoch)` after each of 20 epochs inside one run. Which TWO statements describe how MLflow stores these values? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Calling `log_metric` with an existing key replaces the earlier value, so only the final loss is kept
The parameter is a numeric time series that MLflow updates automatically whenever the optimizer changes the learning rate
Metric values must be strings so that MLflow can compare them across runs with `filter_string`
Each of the 20 loss values is kept together with its step, so the run can show a loss curve
The parameter is stored as a string, and logging the same key again with a different value in that run raises an error

stem: A training script finishes with `mlflow.log_artifact("model.pkl")` for a pickled scikit-learn estimator. A colleague asks why the team should use `mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", input_example=X.head(5))` instead. Which is the best reason?

choices.text: `log_artifact` cannot store files bigger than a few megabytes, while `log_model` has no such restriction
`log_artifact` stores the file in Unity Catalog automatically, while `log_model` leaves the file unversioned in the run
`log_model` saves the MLflow Model format with flavors, dependency files and a signature, so it can be loaded, registered and served
`log_model` stores the model only inside the Databricks control plane, while `log_artifact` copies the file into the customer's cloud storage account

stem: A notebook defines `params = {"max_depth": 8, "n_estimators": 200, "min_samples_leaf": 5}` and `scores = {"rmse": 0.41, "r2": 0.88}`. Which pair of calls records each dictionary in the active run as parameters and metrics, in one call each?

choices.text: `mlflow.log_dict(params, "p.json")` and `mlflow.log_dict(scores, "s.json")`
`mlflow.log_artifacts(params)` and `mlflow.log_artifacts(scores)`
`mlflow.log_params(params)` and `mlflow.log_metrics(scores)`
`mlflow.set_tags(params)` and `mlflow.set_tags(scores)`

stem: A hyperparameter search wraps each trial as `with mlflow.start_run():` inside a function that is itself called inside another `with mlflow.start_run():` block. The first trial raises "Run with UUID ... is already active". The team wants each trial to appear as its own run grouped under the outer run. What is the correct change?

choices.text: Start each trial with `mlflow.start_run(nested=True)`, which creates a child run under the active parent run
Call `mlflow.end_run()` after the outer `start_run`, so that trials never have an active parent
Pass `mlflow.start_run(run_name=...)` with a unique name for each trial, which lets MLflow open several active runs
Set a different experiment with `mlflow.set_experiment` inside each trial, so each trial gets its own active run

stem: An engineer opens the page of one finished run in the MLflow UI on Databricks and wants to check which exact version of the code produced it and what plots the run saved. Which parts of the run page provide this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The Metrics table, which stores the plots as base64 text in each row
The Artifacts tab, which lists logged files such as plots and the logged model
The Spark UI link, which lists the SQL query plans that fed the run
The Permissions button, which shows every user who ever viewed the run
The Source link, which opens the notebook version that launched the run

stem: On an experiment page, a team wants to list only runs whose R2 is above 0.3 and that were tagged as `estimator_name="RandomForestRegressor"`. Which search expression do they enter in the search field?

choices.text: `params.r2 > 0.3 AND params.estimator_name="RandomForestRegressor"`
`SELECT * FROM runs WHERE r2 > 0.3 AND estimator_name = 'RandomForestRegressor'`
`r2 > 0.3, RandomForestRegressor`
`metrics.r2 > 0.3 AND tags.estimator_name="RandomForestRegressor"`

stem: Three data scientists each train in their own notebook and call `mlflow.start_run()` without setting an experiment. The team lead wants all their runs to land in one experiment so the runs can be compared side by side. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Merge the three notebooks into one notebook, because only runs started in the same notebook can be compared
Copy the runs between the notebook experiments by exporting CSV files and re-importing them as new runs
Rely on the defaults, because Databricks groups the runs of notebooks in the same folder into one experiment
Have each notebook call `mlflow.set_experiment("/Shared/churn-model")` first, so every run goes to one shared workspace experiment

stem: A colleague deleted three runs from an experiment page two days ago by mistake, and the team now needs their results. What can the team do in the MLflow UI?

choices.text: Set the State filter to Deleted and restore the runs, because deleted runs stay recoverable for 30 days
Open the colleague's trash folder in the workspace browser, because deleted runs are moved there next to the notebooks
Re-run all three trials, because MLflow keeps only run names and parameter values for deleted runs
Nothing; deleting a run removes its parameters, metrics and artifacts at once and cannot be reversed

stem: A team created a workspace experiment with an artifact location `s3://team-bucket/ml-artifacts`. Runs show parameters and metrics in the MLflow UI, but the Artifacts tab is empty, and registering the logged model fails. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Workspace experiments accept only metrics and parameters, so no artifact file can be logged to such an experiment at all
Artifacts appear only after the experiment is shared with the Unity Catalog metastore admin group
Artifacts kept outside MLflow-managed storage or a Unity Catalog volume are not shown in the UI, and their models cannot be registered
The run was logged to a notebook experiment instead, which hides every file of the run

stem: A model was logged in a run and is ready to be registered. The workspace uses Unity Catalog, and the registered model should be called `churn_model` in the `ml_team` schema of the `prod` catalog. Which call registers it?

choices.text: `mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "ml_team.churn_model")`
`mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "prod.ml_team.churn_model")`
`mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "prod.ml_team.churn_model/1")`, because the trailing number sets the version to create
`mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "prod/ml_team/churn_model")`

stem: On a cluster with MLflow 2 in a workspace whose default catalog is `hive_metastore`, a notebook calls `mlflow.register_model(uri, "prod.ml_team.churn_model")` and fails, because the client tries to use the workspace model registry. What should be added before registering?

choices.text: `mlflow.autolog(disable=True)`, because autologging forces models into the workspace registry
`mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")`, which points the client at the Unity Catalog model registry
`mlflow.set_experiment("prod.ml_team")`, because the experiment path selects the catalog for the model
`mlflow.set_tracking_uri("databricks-uc")`, because the tracking URI selects the model registry

stem: A data scientist needs to create a brand-new registered model in the schema `prod.ml_team` for the first time. The catalog and schema already exist and the user owns neither. Besides `USE CATALOG` on the catalog, which TWO privileges does the user need? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `CREATE MODEL` on the schema
`CREATE TABLE` on the schema, because a model is stored as a table
`MODIFY` on the metastore, because every new securable object needs a metastore-level write privilege
`EXECUTE` on the catalog, because registering needs permission to run models
`USE SCHEMA` on the schema

stem: A script logs a scikit-learn model with `mlflow.sklearn.log_model(clf, name="model")` and then registers it in Unity Catalog. Registration is rejected because the new model version lacks a required item. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Rename the model with a four-level name that includes the workspace, so the missing item is added by the workspace
Log the model again as a plain artifact with `log_artifact`, which has no registration requirements
Log it with an `input_example` (or an explicit signature), or use autologging, so the model version has a signature
Ask a metastore admin to disable the check, because a model signature is only a recommendation in Unity Catalog

stem: A job trains five candidate models in separate runs and must register only the winner. On MLflow 3 the best run's logged model has the URI stored in `best_uri` (of the form `models:/<model_id>`). Which approach registers only that model into Unity Catalog?

choices.text: Call `mlflow.register_model("runs:/<experiment_id>/model", "prod.ml_team.churn")` using the experiment ID
Call `client.create_registered_model(best_uri)`, which registers the model and creates its first version
Log every candidate with `registered_model_name="prod.ml_team.churn"`, then delete the four weaker model versions
Call `mlflow.register_model(best_uri, "prod.ml_team.churn")` after comparing the runs

stem: A dev workspace and a prod workspace share one Unity Catalog metastore. An ML engineer in dev wants to compare a newly trained model with the model currently in production, which was registered from the prod workspace. Which statement about Models in Unity Catalog describes the benefit?

choices.text: The engineer must export the model from prod and import it into dev, since each workspace keeps a private copy of the registry
The engineer must register the new model in the prod workspace first, since a registry is bound to the workspace of its training
The engineer can load the prod model from the dev workspace, given the right privileges, because the registry is governed at the metastore level
The engineer can read the prod model only if both workspaces use the same cluster policy

stem: A company must show auditors who is allowed to load a customer-risk model, trace the model to the tables it was trained on, and grant that access to groups rather than individual users. Which registry choice supports this best?

choices.text: The Workspace Model Registry, because stage names such as Production already encode who is allowed to load the model
A Delta table with one row per model, because tables are the only securable objects that support lineage
A model file in a shared Git folder, because Git history lists every user who has read access
Models in Unity Catalog, with `EXECUTE` granted to groups, audit logs for access, and lineage from the training tables

stem: A team migrating from the Workspace Model Registry (the legacy registry, which used stages) to Unity Catalog asks which statement about the two is correct.

choices.text: The workspace registry shares models across all workspaces of an account, while Unity Catalog models stay in the workspace of their creator
Unity Catalog models use three-level names with versions and aliases, while the workspace registry uses plain names and stages
Both registries offer the same stage transitions, so code that sets a version to Production works unchanged
Models in Unity Catalog use two-level names, while the workspace registry requires three-level names with a catalog

stem: A team starts a new project in a recently created Databricks account whose workspace has a Unity Catalog default catalog. A teammate suggests using the Workspace Model Registry because it is familiar. What does Databricks documentation say about this plan?

choices.text: Databricks disabled the Workspace Model Registry for new accounts whose default catalog is in Unity Catalog, and recommends Unity Catalog models
Unity Catalog models are allowed there only for tables, so models must be stored as Delta tables instead
It works the same as in older accounts, because both registries are fully supported in every new workspace and the choice is only a matter of habit
The registry is available only in the Unity Catalog metastore admin console and needs a per-user opt-in

stem: A team on MLflow 3 in a Unity Catalog workspace runs `mlflow.register_model(uri, "prod.ml_team.churn_model")` with no registry configuration and the model appears in Catalog Explorer. A teammate wants to explain why no `set_registry_uri` call was needed. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: MLflow 3 copies every registered model to both registries, so the model is also present in the legacy workspace registry as a stage-less copy
MLflow 3 hides the workspace registry completely, so `set_registry_uri("databricks")` can no longer be called
In MLflow 3 the default registry URI is `databricks-uc`, so models go to Unity Catalog unless the registry URI is changed
Catalog Explorer lists workspace registry models too, so the model there came from the workspace registry

stem: A Spark ML `ParamGridBuilder` defines 3 values of `regParam` and 4 values of `maxIter`. The grid is passed to a `CrossValidator` with `numFolds=5`. How many model fits does the search itself run, not counting the final refit on the full dataset?

choices.text: 61, the search fits plus one fit for the final best model
20, one fit for each fold and each `maxIter` value
12, one fit for each combination of `regParam` and `maxIter`
60, one fit for each combination in each of the five folds

stem: A data scientist builds a grid of 3 values for `numTrees` and 2 values for `maxDepth` and tunes a Spark ML `RandomForestRegressor` with `TrainValidationSplit`. How many models are fitted in total, including the final model trained with the best parameters on the whole dataset?

choices.text: 3, one fit for each value of `numTrees`
7, six combination fits plus the final fit on the entire dataset
6, one fit for each of the parameter combinations
12, each combination is fitted twice, once for training and once for validation

stem: A team's grid had 4 values of `maxDepth` and 3 values of `minInstancesPerNode`, evaluated with 3 folds. They now add two more `minInstancesPerNode` values (5 in total) and move to 5 folds. How many fits does the search run now, not counting the refit?

choices.text: 100, since 4 x 5 combinations are each fitted in 5 folds
20, since only the 4 x 5 combinations are counted once each
36, since 4 x 3 combinations are each fitted in 3 folds
60, since 4 x 3 combinations are each fitted in 5 folds

stem: A grid search over three hyperparameters with 4 values each runs with `CrossValidator(numFolds=5)`, which is too slow. Which TWO changes bring the number of search fits below 100? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Set `collectSubModels=True` and keep the same grid and folds
Set `parallelism=8` and keep the same grid and folds
Keep the grid and folds and add a second evaluator metric
Switch to `TrainValidationSplit` and keep the same grid
Cut each hyperparameter to 3 values and use 3 folds

stem: A Spark ML `CrossValidator` is fitted with 6 `ParamMap`s and `numFolds=3`, and the data scientist inspects `cvModel.avgMetrics`. What does this attribute contain?

choices.text: 1 value, the metric of the best model after it is refit on the entire dataset
6 values, one for each parameter combination, each averaged over the three folds
18 values, one for every model fit in the search, in the order the fits ran
3 values, one for each fold, each averaged over all six parameter combinations

stem: A team scores a binary classifier with Spark ML `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` and wants the area under the precision-recall curve instead of the default metric. Which `metricName` do they set?

choices.text: `areaUnderPR`, the area under the precision-recall curve
`prAUC`, a short name for the area under the precision-recall curve
`f1`, the harmonic mean of precision and recall
`areaUnderRecall`, the area under the recall curve

stem: A multiclass model outputs class probabilities, and the team wants its log loss with Spark ML. Which setup computes it?

choices.text: `RegressionEvaluator(metricName="mse")` on the label and predicted class index columns
`BinaryClassificationEvaluator(metricName="logLoss")` on `label` and `rawPrediction` columns
`MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(metricName="logLoss")` on `label` and `probability` columns
`MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(metricName="logLoss")` on `label` and `prediction` columns

stem: A classifier reaches precision 0.90 and recall 0.30 for the positive class. What is its F1 score for that class?

choices.text: 0.90, the precision, because F1 follows the higher value
0.60, the arithmetic mean of precision and recall
0.27, the product of precision and recall
0.45, the harmonic mean of precision and recall

stem: A team passes the hard 0/1 `prediction` column of a classifier as the `rawPredictionCol` of `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` with the default metric. On the validation set the true positive rate is 0.80 and the true negative rate is 0.90. What does the evaluator return?

choices.text: 0.85, the average of the two rates
An error, because the column must hold a vector of scores
0.72, the product of the two rates
0.90, the larger of the two rates

stem: Two binary classifiers both reach 90% accuracy at a 0.5 threshold. Model X's wrong predictions have probabilities near 0.5. Model Y's wrong predictions have probabilities near 0.99 for the wrong class. Which metric separates the models, and which model does it favor?

choices.text: `areaUnderROC`, which scores model Y higher because its errors are more extreme
`hammingLoss`, which favors model Y because its wrong predictions are further away

F1 at the 0.5 threshold, which favors model Y because its errors are more confident

stem: A Spark ML `RegressionEvaluator` is created without setting `metricName`. Which metric does `evaluate` return?

choices.text: `mae`, the mean absolute error
`rmse`, the root mean squared error
`r2`, the coefficient of determination
`mse`, the mean squared error

stem: A delivery-time model makes five errors of 1, 1, 1, 1 and 16 minutes (absolute values) on a validation set. Which statement about its MAE and RMSE is correct?

choices.text: MAE and RMSE are both 4, because both average the errors the same way
MAE is 20 and RMSE is about 7.2, because MAE sums the five errors
MAE is about 7.2 and RMSE is 4, because MAE weights the 16-minute miss more heavily
MAE is 4 and RMSE is about 7.2, because squaring gives the 16-minute miss a large weight

stem: A regression model evaluated on a validation set returns an `r2` of -0.3. What does the value say?

choices.text: The model explains 30% of the variance with the opposite sign of the relation
The model fits worse than always predicting the mean of the validation labels
The model's average error is 30% of the mean label value
The evaluation is invalid because R-squared must be between 0 and 1

stem: Which statement correctly compares RMSE and MAE for the same predictions?

choices.text: Both are in the label's units, and RMSE is never smaller than MAE
MAE is measured in squared units of the label and punishes outliers more
RMSE is unitless and always lies between 0 and 1
RMSE is robust to outliers because it averages the squared residuals

stem: A `CrossValidator` uses `RegressionEvaluator(metricName="rmse")`. How does it pick the best `ParamMap`?

choices.text: The one with the lowest RMSE in the first fold only
The one with the highest RMSE averaged across folds
The one with the lowest RMSE averaged over folds, as smaller is better here
The one with the highest R-squared, because `r2` is the metric of every evaluator

stem: A fraud model flags card transactions, and only 0.3% of the rows are fraud. The team cares about finding fraud among the flagged cases and wants one threshold-free score for comparing candidates. Which metric fits best?

RMSE between the predicted class and the label
`areaUnderPR` from the binary evaluator
`hammingLoss` across all transactions

stem: A screening model flags patients for a follow-up test. Missing a sick patient is far more costly than a false alarm, which only triggers an extra test. Which metric should the team prioritize?

choices.text: Precision of the positive class
Recall of the positive class
True negative rate (specificity)
Weighted precision across the classes

stem: A spam filter moves flagged mail into a folder that users rarely open. Losing a legitimate message is much worse than letting some spam through. Which metric should be optimized?

choices.text: Precision of the spam class
Mean absolute error of the spam score
Overall accuracy across the legitimate and spam classes
Recall of the spam class

stem: A team forecasts delivery times in minutes. A handful of records have wrong timestamps that create extreme values, and the team does not want them to dominate the choice among models. They also want the score in minutes. Which `RegressionEvaluator` metric fits?

choices.text: `mse`, because it is in minutes squared
`r2`, because it is unitless
`rmse`, because squaring emphasizes the extreme errors
`mae`, because it weighs every error linearly

stem: A binary classifier is trained on data with about 1% positives. Which TWO metrics give useful information about how well it finds the positive class? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `hammingLoss` from `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator`
`weightedTruePositiveRate`, which weights each class by its share of the rows
Overall accuracy at the 0.5 threshold
`areaUnderPR` from `BinaryClassificationEvaluator`
`fMeasureByLabel` for label 1.0

stem: A model is trained on `log(revenue)` as its label. In which situation must the predictions be exponentiated before they are used?

choices.text: Residuals against fitted values are plotted to check whether the spread is even
Two candidates are ranked by their RMSE on the log scale on one shared validation set
Finance wants predicted revenue in currency and an RMSE measured in currency
Feature importance scores are compared between two trained models

stem: Model L is trained on `log(price)` and reports an RMSE of 0.21. Model R is trained on raw price and reports an RMSE of 48,000 dollars. A colleague says L is clearly better because 0.21 is smaller. What is the right response?

choices.text: Disagree: apply `exp` to L's predictions and recompute RMSE against original prices
Multiply L's RMSE by 100,000 so that it is on the same scale as R
Take the logarithm of R's RMSE so that it is on the same scale as L
Agree, since a smaller RMSE always means the better model, whatever the target is

stem: A target with many zero values was transformed with `np.log1p(y)` before training. Which function converts the model's predictions back to the original scale?

choices.text: `np.exp(x)`, since the exponential is the inverse of a logarithm
`np.expm1(x)`, which computes exp(x) - 1
`np.exp(x) + 1`, which adds back the shift
`np.log1p(x)`, applied a second time to undo the shift

stem: A Spark ML regression model was trained on `log1p(sales)`. Which TWO steps give an RMSE in the original sales units? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Evaluate against the original, untransformed sales column
Evaluate against the log1p label to avoid a mismatch
Apply `log1p` to the prediction column again
Apply `expm1` to the feature columns before scoring
Apply `expm1` to the prediction column

stem: A linear regression is fit on `log(price)`, and the coefficient for `bedrooms` is 0.05. How should the team interpret it for price?

Each extra bedroom adds about 1.05 currency units to the predicted price

stem: A Spark ML `RandomForestRegressor` with `maxDepth=30` has a training RMSE of 2.1 and a validation RMSE of 14.8. What does this pattern show, and what is the sensible next step?

choices.text: Irreducible noise only; no change to the model can help
High bias (underfitting); increase model complexity and add polynomial features
High bias; train longer on the same training rows
High variance (overfitting); reduce complexity or add regularization and more data

stem: A linear regression has a training RMSE of 11.9 and a validation RMSE of 12.3 on data with a clearly curved relationship. Which diagnosis and fix fit?

choices.text: High variance; strengthen the regularization of the linear model and shrink coefficients
High bias (underfitting); add polynomial features or move to a more flexible model
Perfect fit; no change is needed because both errors are close
High variance; collect fewer features and train on fewer rows to reduce complexity

stem: A Spark ML `RandomForestClassifier` overfits: training accuracy is near 100% and validation accuracy is much lower. Which TWO changes lower its variance? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Increase `maxDepth` and decrease `minInstancesPerNode`
Increase `minInstancesPerNode`
Monitor training accuracy only and stop when it reaches 100%
Add more features that repeat existing columns
Decrease `maxDepth`

stem: A team fits polynomial regressions of degree 1 to 8. Training RMSE keeps falling as the degree grows. Validation RMSE is 9.0, 6.1, 4.8, 4.2, 4.5, 5.9, 8.3, 11.0 for degrees 1 to 8. Which degree should the team choose, and why?

choices.text: Degree 4, because it has the lowest validation RMSE
Degree 1, because the simplest model is always the best
